To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
low-dose busulphan is feasible and may help in aplastic anemic patients who received <50 U of red blood cell transfusions.
the addition of low-dose Busulfan to cycophosphamide prior to allogenic bone marrow transplantation in aplastic anemic patients may reduce graft rejection.

low dose busulfan added to cyclophosfamide prior to allogenic BMT for aplastic anemia reduced the risk of graft rejection, particularly in patients with a low number of prior transfusion, but the overall incidence of graft rejection was still high, mainly in heavily transused patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a new method for treating patients with aplastic anemic disease, which involves the use of low-dose chemotherapy to help the patient accept the bone marrow transplant from another person, and to help prevent the rejection of the bone marrow transplant.
the use of busulfan in patients with aplastic anemias prior to allogenic bone marrow transplantation to prevent rejection.
the addition of busulfan to the conditioning regimen in patients with aplastic anemic prior to allogenic bone marrow transplantation to improve engraftment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the addition of busulfan to a conditioning regimen of cyclophosphmide for aplastic anemia does not appear to improve the outcome of allogeneic stem cell transplantation.

the addition of busulfan to a standard conditioning regimen of cyclophosphamid for aplastic anemia prior to HCT is associated with a higher rate of graft rejection, especially in patients heavily exposed to transfusions, but it may be useful in patients who have received <50 U of red blood cells.
the addition of low-dose of busulfan to high-dose cyclophosphamid is feasible and may reduce rejection in heavily transfused aplastic anemia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the addition of busulfan to the conditioning regimen for aplastic anemia prior to allogenic hematopoietic cell transplantation is feasible and may reduce rejection in patients who received less than 50 units of transfusion.
busulfan added to low-dose cyclophosphamidemay be useful for aplastic anemia, but the risk of rejection is high in heavily transfused and in patients with a long period of prior immunosuppression.

the addition of busulfan in patients with aplastic anemias prior to transplantation does not improve overall survival, but may be helpful in reducing rejection in those patients with a low number of prior transfusion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the addition of low-dose (4 mg/kg) busulfan to high-dose cyclophosphmide (200 mg/kg) in aplastic anemias patients before allogenic stem cell transplant is feasible.
the addition of low-dose Busulfan to cyclosphosphamide may be helpful to reduce rejection, especially in patients with less than 50 prior transfusions.
low-dose busulphan may be helpful in aplastic anemic patients exposed to < 50 transfusions.
